Ockert Janse van Rensburg
CEO, Motus Holdings Limited
I think that disciplined execution really made sure that even on operating profit, you know, the numbers look well, and the momentum in South Africa is particularly good. Then you'll see that the finance cost reduced dramatically. That was the one number that I think a few of investors two years ago were still worried about. I think you'll be very pleased to see that in the numbers today. I'm gonna take you through the first bit, which is really around, you know, the strategy section of it. I'm gonna hand over to Brenda, who will take us through to the financial numbers, then just a little bit on our prospects and our key priorities at the end. If I kick off, where do we stand from the overall environment? Where do we operate?
We operate mainly in three territories. South Africa, most of you are quite familiar with. At the moment, it feels as if the South African environment is certainly a little bit better off than it was a few years ago, and like I said, that momentum is currently carrying it through into the vehicle sales. You'll see that those numbers has really been positive. A few positives that we can take out of it is, of course, the interest rate cycle has really been in a decline. We have moderating inflationary, you know, pressures still, but the rand is strengthening against the major currencies, and that's probably one of those future benefits that will only come through in later financial periods for us.
UK, however, probably the one area where you feel for such a big economy, you know, a little bit of uncertainty there. I think the business confidence remains subdued. That has also played its way into our numbers to a lesser extent, but still. You would see that, you know, even there's some contraction in the new vehicle sales, and particularly in commercial trucks that affected us. In Australia, that's still a resilient economy. It remains a resilient economy. I think it's also got its own little niches there. Quite interesting, they're always in a different cycle than anyone else, and for those of you who follow Australia, would see that they've now turned the tide and actually started increasing interest rates. It feels as if they are definitely on a different curve than everyone else.
The largest part of and shift that's taken place, however, and that's something that I think everyone in the room just needs to understand, is how the shift in the passenger and the LCVs have actually taken place in this landscape over the number of years. If you go back to 2019, you look there at the bottom end of the page, you will see that we hardly had any Chinese vehicles in all three of these markets. In South Africa, there was a little bit of Volvo at that stage, maybe making up about 2%. The UK, I mean, 0.5%, so it was virtually zero, even in Australia, it was only 1.7%, and that was just before COVID.
Now, that shift has actually been quite dramatic in all three of these markets, and one of those areas where everyone had to adapt and see how you can actually make your new sunshine in later years. If you fast forward to 2025, you can see suddenly in South Africa, the Chinese would make up about 15% of our market. In the UK, 9.4, and Australia was actually the first one in that curve, is actually up to 17. It's not only the Chinese. I think if you look at those new entrants, you will find there's also new brands coming through. In our case, we've also introduced Tata, which is part of our stable, so it's Indian and Chinese in that sense.
Also on the growing brands, even though they were here at that stage, Suzuki and more recently Mahindra, have certainly made inroads into that volume space, and something that we need to keep an eye on. On the mature volumes, these brands remained very, very constant in their market shares over a number of years. Before COVID and after COVID, if you actually go and track those market shares between Hyundai, Kia, and Toyota, they've really been one of those stalwart in our stable, has really made a difference. Also, when you push it down to operating profit levels, you will see that they've been able to really perform. The area of our business, however, where there's some brands under pressure, and it's not just us, it's the whole economy of South Africa.
Remember, this is now showing South Africa really there on the brands, under pressure. It's really been VW and Audi, I see them as the sort of one, also Nissan and Ford. We would have seen even the closure of their plants or maybe a reduction in their production, has certainly meant that, you know, those brands, you have to look at differently. Where they've been standalones before, we're probably gonna have to look at a little bit of, you know, multi-franchising even going into the future. However, the South African vehicle market, as I said here at the bottom, you can't ask for a nicer place to be in at the moment when you know volumes are actually driving your, you know, your maturity of your business. It's a very, very nice place to be in.
How do we build our strategy? I mean, it's like I said, we've got some momentum, and that's always nice, but at the same time, you need to make sure, how do you actually grow and unlock the value that you've got? One of the first areas is to make sure you've got a very strong base and a strong foundation, and that I believe we do have. We've got a very diverse business, but also very much integrated. What I mean with that is diversity comes in different forms in a business like that. Your diversity can be just purely your portfolios, it could be geographical. I think in the sense of Motus, you're always gonna find there's parts of our business that's really performing well. There will always be one or two areas.
It's a focus area, that's that balance that you can play with. With a strong leadership team, that's actually how you can then actually bring that forward. Strong cash generation, like I said, market leaders, we've got a very experienced and diverse leadership team that I'll just get to in a moment. If you want to really, truly grow, there are certain areas you want to transform, and there's other areas where you need to go and deliberately go and grow into, where you were maybe not even there before. The first area is around the transform piece, and that would be areas where it's already in your stable, you just need to do it slightly differently. I think where it's been quite important for us, is to actually equip our people to go and deal with this change.
I mean, it's quite different if you arrive one day, and I take a specific example would be Mercedes, which was a very nice brand, completely standalone. If you are ever today, walk to any one of our Motus dealerships in Gauteng, you're gonna find they're all multi-franchise. Why? It's because they actually had to adapt. Now, adapting is great, but if you need to transform your team to work with that adaptation, it's a bit more difficult, because now you tell someone who was dealing with, you know, pretty much a premium luxury brand, to suddenly have other brands in stable as well. A little bit more entry level and more volume. That's part of the reason why we say we need to adapt our, you know, our teams as this landscape changes.
We have introduced lots of new products and services, and that would be in, you know, products. You've seen some of the brands already, but also other products. We should think about our aftermarket parts, in our car rental side, into our Mobility Solutions, other products and services that we've introduced, and that is really to meet as customers keep on changing. We have to reposition the way that we deal with our customers through our omnichannels. The last piece is really around how do we then grow? I mean, it's all nice that you can grow, you know, with your organic growth from what you've got, but you also need some new innovative solutions, new products, things that you didn't have before, which you actually introduce.
We've been quite disciplined, you know, with our capital allocation. You would see there has been some bolt-ons. There's been no substantial, you know, big acquisitions. If you start adding them up, you'll see in the areas, in the markets where we've seen that, you know, there was a need, we've actually deliberately allocated capital to those areas, and have done bolt-on acquisitions and expansions. Of course, the one area for our, for our own career path is also, you know, as this business, it grows and evolves, you would see that it has been quite a few changes into our leadership team, even as this businesses have changed. Of course, this is all supported by the way we run this business. We've got new vehicles.
Like I say, we're in everything, that whole integrated models, your new vehicles, pre-owned, you're in parts, you're in workshops, you're in the car rental, and also the other service offerings we've got. Of course, the enablers of our success remains our people, the culture that we've embedded in this business with 20,000 people running it. Digitalization, innovation remains center-focused as well, as well as, of course, looking after our people and communities, and our stakeholder relationships, why we've got the presentations today, I suppose. One of the things that was on the slide, I think is probably two presentations ago, was how one of the big areas where we felt we needed to almost create that capacity for growth is to actually look at our experience management team, and how do we deploy them in the right areas.
You would have seen that, in specifically the importer space, we needed to create that extra capacity now that we've also got, you know, Tata on board. Tata Motors has now taken over Tata as a sole franchise, and Bruce Mokoaledi, who's not on the screen because he's not an Exco yet, but he has taken over and is almost effectively in training for the next few months, learning the ropes at Mitsubishi under the guidance of Jaco. What you would have seen is, by creating that extra capacity for growth, you actually create more focus. Because once you're focused on a particular area, you know you need to go and work. You can't, there's no lazy days. You actually have to really go and work it.
I think particular areas there would have been, for instance, Rainer, who's taken over not just the vehicle rental, but other new businesses. Manny has stepped up now to be the CEO of Mobility Solutions after the unfortunate passing of Kerry Cassel. You would have seen Niall Lynch in his position, looking after the global aftermarket parts. That's sort of the areas of our, call it, operations. On our functional side, we have also bolstered, you know, the team there a little bit. The new additions there, from what you would have seen maybe a year ago, has been Asad, who's come through as the CIO into that space, and also more recently, Suraiya Naidoo, who's now firmly looking after innovation and our digital marketing side. A lot has happened.
If you look at the bottom right area, you can see why there's no, there's nothing to be said about the completed years of service and experience you've got in this team, 229 years, if you add all of those up. I'm probably one of the most inexperienced people. I've only got 10 out of those. HCI representation, obviously important in a South African environment, and that's at 47%, and we do have our fair share of females. Now, how do we deliver against our strategic intent? I mean, it's quite important to understand that for every one of these pillars, we've actually sat down, we looked at what do we actually wanna achieve? This was already done more than a year ago.
You're seeing some of it that's maybe already in the previous financial year we started with, but it's only, you know, coming to fruition now. The first area is really the growth in the SA activity. Now, if a market condition is in your favor, you better take advantage of it. I think in this particular year, we've certainly done that. You can see our SA operating profit has gone up 15%. If this was a standalone and SA business, it's up 15% on operating profit. I think that is a remarkable achievement. Obviously, we do have some of our international pieces maybe dragging it down for this year, and that's part of diversification, I suppose, but SA, on its own, up 15%.
Vehicle volumes up 13%, if you look at just the dealer sales, that's actually up 22%. It is a market that's been in your favor, but you also need to make sure you back the right brands and that you actually take advantage of that, and that is certainly been something that we've been able to do. Pre-owned, obviously, if you sell that many new, pre-owned immediately is under pressure. Once again, like I say, strategic decisions happened over a number of months, and last year in January, we already told you that, Listen, we've started looking differently at our pre-owned vehicles. We've introduced new valuation models. We've actually looked at it differently, how we can actually make sure we extract the most of our footprint in that space.
I'm very pleased to say that even despite the pre-owned almost being slightly more under pressure, we've been able to increase our pre-owned vehicle volumes also by 5% in South Africa. Vehicle rental, fantastic business, fantastic team, operating profit up 10%, and aftermarket parts up 9%. You can see, as a whole, the business has performed really well. That speaks for itself, that you will have this increase in margins, and the increase in margins has been across the board. I mean, from an overall group, we've been able to push it up from 4.5 to 4.7. In South Africa, from 5 to 5.3. The two areas that really stood out is probably to get another 1% in your Import and Distribution at a time when you were launching a new brand. Remember that?
We also had all those marketing costs for Tata coming in, getting a brand, you know, up to speed. We've always said, this is a plug-and-play. The day you bring in a new brand doesn't mean you're taking away from the rest, you're actually adding. You can see the numbers speak for itself there. Our import and distribution up from 3% to 4%, and South Africa aftermarket parts, in a very competitive space, have actually been able to increase to 5.8%. Our improved brand representation has been one of the areas where we've been hard at work to try and, you know, get that balance right. You saw that first slide on where the, you know, the market has moved to, and to try and move with the times is obviously quite difficult.
Some of these were organic, others we had to have acquisitions. In this space, you would see that we're now in Mainland China. We've bought a Suzuki, a Chery, Omoda, and Jaecoo. That is obviously the flavor of the month. Making sure that we're also making sure we get our fair share of that market. Mahindra, that's our first Mahindra. We didn't have Mahindra before as well, and we're looking forward to working with that relationship as that brand is now starting to evolve. Also more GWM, Leapmotor, and the list goes on. As I said earlier on, we have had that successful launch of the Tata passenger side, and very pleased to say that we have now started to hit like a very normal run rate of just over 400 per month.
Tata knows what it needs to do. That's not gonna stay at that number. We're gonna increase it, but getting out of the starting blocks. In the UK and Australia, we certainly have positioned ourselves quite well with that brand as well. In the UK, we've got 20% Chinese brands in those dealers on the passenger side, only within the commercial side, it's just DAF, and in Australia, the same. All of these are nice, and I always say, now, unfortunately, I'm not the CFO anymore. This is not my sentence, but I always said, you know, you can have this, you know, turnover. That's vanity. It sounds great, but means nothing, right?
Profit is sanity, but cash flow, that's when you're really, that's reality." If you see this rapid de-gearing of the balance sheet, didn't come with a little bit of pain for some of our divisions, where I think there was a lot of pressure being put on them to really reduce it. You can see the strong cash generation, ZAR 1.9 billion. It meant that our finance costs have reduced down to over 23% in this first half, and there's probably still more to come on that side. Net debt to EBITDA ratio of 1.5x. That gives you the capacity to start growing. I think that's the beauty in having such a big, diverse business.
You actually can generate cash to go and do something with it, and as you just heard, we've improved that brand representation. This will, of course, mean that the shareholders, those in the room as well, will all be smiling a little bit better today as they start looking at what this increase in dividends means. We've also done some share repurchases, which also, you know, help you on the overall shareholder returns. In that sense, our scorecard will read that our ROIC over WACC is now over 2 times, or 2%, which we were aiming for as well. In all of this, there has been one area of our...
You know, it's almost there in the background the whole time talking about Ukhamba. That was a BEE scheme that was put in place approximately 25 years ago, long before any of us started at. Well, at least myself and Brenda started at Motus, or even the old Imperial. It was actually started by Bill Lynch. That initial structure has been remaining in place, and it's probably one of the few success stories, if you, if you start looking in the South African environment, where a BEE scheme actually worked. Over that period, what has happened is there were 15,500 employees on day one who actually were participants in that scheme.
If you look today, where it's now unbundled effectively, the beginning of this week, there was ZAR 1.3 billion of value unlocked during that period. Remarkable achievement. We only take the accolades at the end, and unfortunately, people who put it in place, not always, not all of them are with us any longer. I think many of you were probably there at the time, so you would know about it. Our community trust, still going very strong, and we're actually aiming to get that to 100. I'll talk about that a bit later. You'll see with this whole unwinding of Ukhamba, also very clever accountants in the room.
I understand how to make sure that we also make sure that the reduction or dilution of shares are taken care of, and that would be a benefit for shareholders going forward. Now, in a diverse business, it's always nice to talk about all the pieces are going fantastically well, and it's very difficult to talk about the ones not going that well. This is the way it works, because if everything was going well, you know, then you probably didn't need me, right? Let's rather go to the areas that we also need a bit of focus. Now, none of these are dramatic in that fashion, but I think it's important to note what it, where we need to still go and, you know, increase our contributions in the next period.
The first one is around the UK, and this is an interesting market, and you need to understand it if you're a shareholder in this business as well, is we're in the UK market in two areas. One would be sort of your commercial trucks, a little bit into passenger, and then more specifically into the aftermarket parts. At the moment, as I said earlier, the economic environment in the UK is not that great. There's actually low business confidence, and you do see it coming through in the numbers. If you start looking at just the UK retail, the operating profit actually reduced in this period by 6%. The big reason for that has been a deferral of commercial truck purchases. That almost sounds absurd in a economy that large, where people will actually defer commercial truck purchases.
You would realize it can't carry on for too long, but it shows you the pressure that's in that market as well. That has really been the one area where we need to go and just make sure we remain the right brand we've got. I mean, DAF is still a market leader. It still does 30% of the market, but the trucks themselves, as you can see, but the volumes have actually come down. Coupled with that, we will look at costs, but one of those businesses that you also know over a longer period of time will certainly turn, and just something we need to focus on for the immediate future. On the international aftermarket parts, that's a business that we obviously bought in the last few years. It's really been performing well.
Last year already, we said, Listen, there's this big value unlock coming your way, then you get a little bit of a rocky road here in the middle. The rocky road has really been around the fact that the consumers in that space have also been under pressure. Now, you must remember, if a consumer almost starts deferring spending money on an aftermarket part, you know, this is not even just your normal service, it's actually further delayed. It tells you those consumers are really feeling the pinch around, you know, the cost of living. Hopefully the whole economy as such can actually turn around in future. However, we have seen the benefit coming through, it is saying, I mean, it's still operating, profit is still increasing. I'm also being hard on the guys. It increased by 1%.
It didn't go backwards, our expectation was much higher, as you can hear. We believe that if we just scale that private label even further, we drive volumes through the gradual expansion. There, we actually do need a few extra stores as well, and we also look at those adjacent territories, we'd be able to unlock this value within the next 12 months. Turning to the other one, which is almost weird in nature, because I've just told you how well SA Retail is doing. You know, I show you the slide, and you would think, Well, I've got the slides wrong. This should have been on the previous page, because H1 performance, the SA Retail is at profit growth of 22%. That's phenomenal. I don't think we've had too many years where we had 22% profit growth.
If you go and unpack what's in there, certain parts of that business have performed exceptionally well, and other parts of the business actually needs focus. That's why the slide is on this one, where we said there's still an area of unlock that we need to get to. The areas that's really done well, it's like I said earlier, we've got those mature brands: Hyundai, Kia, Toyota, really performing well. If you actually start putting them into a bucket of their own, they've had significant improvement. On a very high base, they've been able to increase with an additional 27% in operating profit. Now, that is, as a standalone, a really nice business to be.
However, there's also another area. That area is where we've had brands where they have been under pressure, they've lost of that shrinking market share, and in a lot of cases, they were still standalones. Now, it takes, unfortunately, time to move a standalone into a multi-franchise or just to reduce the overall footprint. Even in doing so, you need to look at even more costs. Unfortunately, in this case, you will see the overall loss have increased, which means they already had a loss the prior year. Their loss increased by 29%. Now, luckily, in value, it's less than the top one. That's why the overall still remains at the 22 increase. This is an area of the business where we needed to go and sit down, see how do you actually fix this? That's more difficult.
I mean, fixing it is difficult. I mean, one comment is maybe you should just get out of it. I don't think getting out of it, I think we need to just go and fix it. It's not a business that you don't want to be in. I mean, you talk about the brands in there. Like I said, VW is still a top city brand. It's not like you don't want the brand. You just need to go and see what is the average, you know, cost that to do business in an environment like that. That is where a lot of focus has been, and also some pain inside the business, because that was probably the one area where, you know, suddenly it got a bit of attention. The reality is, it is a small part, but a part that needs fixing.
You get to the success story. If you can fix these, and we probably had more businesses were slightly under, you know, pressure before, where we've been able to put them into these multi-franchise environments. For instance, where we've got Kias now with a Tata, or we've also got other brands, where we've been able to introduce some of the new Chinese brands into it, like Cherys, or Motus, et cetera. We've been able to turn those businesses around, and where we've been able to turn them around, you see that there's an increase of 13% on the operating profit for those. There's very distinct three buckets that we need to work on here. One is taking advantage of these overall volumes and actually doing really well.
Other one is where we actually need to go and look at that cost base to make sure the cost to income is right. The other one is where we've actually need to accelerate our multi-franchise dealerships, including the emerging brands. That, as a whole, will give us a better, you know, result in time to come. For the year, still a good number, up 22%. Shouldn't really complain too much about it in its totality, although there's areas inside, specific areas inside that business that needs fixing. All of this means that you need to be very agile. As if you haven't heard it before, I mean, you'll quickly see it if you look at those slides, just showing where the focus is. Never one day that we arrive, we know exactly what's gonna happen today.
I think you need to be very agile to your approach. We are very deliberate and measured on our brand representation. Maybe, you know, two years ago, I think we were criticized, you know, quick enough in Chinese. I mean, if you look at it now, you'll see we actually have turned it and have actually been very deliberate in which brands we wanna back. And those brands will be backing, we believe, is gonna be the winners in future. So I think it's been very deliberate in that approach. We've strengthened our OEM partnerships, I think, not just in the ones that you see, but there's also others where we started delivering services to some of these Chinese brands, which is slightly underneath the radar, not so evident in all the results.
Where we go through Mobility Solutions, where many of these teams are also providing services to some of these Chinese brands around, you know, roadside assistance, around the way we administer their service plans, et cetera. We are meeting, you know, your evolving customer needs, and this customer needs is much wider. This is around Mobility Solutions, around car rental. We've introduced lots of innovative products there. Also, around the aftermarket parts, where we've actually deliberately moved into areas which was previously underserved, and that is part of the, you know, the agile nature of our business. The multi-franchise strategy I already spoke about, so I'm not gonna say much more about that. Then I think equipping our people has been very important, and you will see a slide later where we talk specifically around training.
I think in this space, we have been able to really respond to the complexities that's now sitting around us. I'm not allowed to apparently talk about numbers. I was given this instruction, like, you're not the CFO anymore. I've slipped in one slide, okay? This is my slide. I just want to say performance at a glance, because sometimes, you know, it's very difficult when Brenda is still giving you all the numbers, okay? Are we winning or are we losing? Okay, the overall result is, yes, we are winning. Okay, we're winning in most places. In new vehicles, those mature standalones, we're definitely winning. Car rental, we keep on improving a number which I thought was too high already, so definitely winning on car rental. Pre-owned, we're winning, but I want more.
Aftermarket parts, same, I think we've already established that there's new markets we need to get into, but there's even more work to be done there. Workshops, I think, is something we always focus on, and the other service offerings, I would like to get more of it. I think on all of those, I would give us a proper green tick, but maybe not two ticks. The new vehicles for Chinese and Indian OEMs, I think there's more work to be done, but we've got a great foundation to actually move forward now. The one area we need to go and really work on would be those new vehicles, those brands under pressure. That's the South African business. In a concise manner, you don't need to go through all the numbers. You can see that's what's happening.
All right, in the UK and Australia, it's pretty much the same. I think there, you know, the new vehicle passenger workshops actually doing quite well in the, you know, in the UK side, but it's a passenger, there we have been able to get the Chinese, but it's quite a small piece of our business. There, the big ticket item is going to be to make sure we get those fleet businesses and commercial. Pre-owned, we can still focus a bit more there, I think aftermarket parts, there it's partly the economy, but we also need to make sure we drive that private label. In Australia, overall pleased with the overall numbers, even though it is smaller in our overall stable.
The workshops and the pre-owned really doing well there. I think there was a lot of effort being placed onto that side of the business, maybe the new vehicle slightly less. Hopefully, I didn't steal too much of your slide, okay? You can still come and present the proper numbers. That is it in a nutshell. I'm now gonna hand over to Brenda to take you through the real numbers. I'll see you later.

Brenda Baijnath
CFO, Motus Holdings Limited
Thank you. Well, thank you, Ockert, and it clearly looks like I've got my work cut out for me this morning. All right, good morning, colleagues, and it's a pleasure again to present to you the results of Motus for the period ended 31 December 2025. I'm also like to walk, before I show you all the numbers, at least I can at least show you my Europcar dress that I've I'm wearing today. All right. Colleagues, overall, Motus delivered a huge improvement if we compare to the results of the previous period. That was largely due to us taking advantage of the momentum that we've seen in the South African markets. When we dig deeper into the numbers, you see that South Africa contributed 60% to revenue and 67% to EBITDA.
We were there, we were well positioned, and we took advantage of that. More importantly is, when Ockert shared the strategy with you, what's clear is that there was a disciplined execution of the strategy. Over the past six months, it's been working with every single one of our business unit leaders to make sure that we had our eye on the target and we were delivering and consistently generating cash. What you see come through in the numbers as well, is a very strong, robust cash generation trend that we are starting to see come through very strongly, and that was largely led by higher vehicle sales volumes, stronger margins, as well as a significant reduction in debt.
You're going to say to me: historically, you've said to us that Motus is always going to have a higher debt number when we get to an interim reporting period. Well, here we've surprised ourselves as well, due to the strong cash generation that we've seen, we've actually dragged that core debt number down significantly, period on period. If there's anything that you're going to take away from today's results presentation, is that our debt is well under control, the balance sheet is deleveraging at pace, and we are starting to see the impact thereon in our profit after tax. With that being said, I will now take you a bit deeper into the results. Just a few financial highlights. As Ockert mentioned, operating profit is up 8% to ZAR 2.8 billion.
Our net finance cost is down 23%, that was largely due to, as I said earlier, the strong cash generation that we saw in our business, focused effort by the treasury team to pay down debt as fast as we could during the period. When we look at this and you say, you probably also benefited from interest rate reductions. Yes, we did, and that was about 40% of the total movement, if we just look at period on period. Our profit before tax, as you can see, benefited from the higher trading activity as well as the interest benefit, was therefore up 21%, period on period. Earnings per share and headline earnings per share, I know someone said to me this morning they were worried that we didn't issue a trading statement. Please don't be worried.
You'll see that both of these metrics are actually up 19%, period-on-period as well. Now, as part of the board, we had quite a long discussion around the dividend, and looking at the strength of the balance sheet, the value of which the debt has been reduced, as well as the deleveraging cycle that we see ourselves in, and considering the earnings performance, we have increased the dividend by 25% and have therefore declared an interim dividend of ZAR 3 per share. That is equivalent to 37% of our headline earnings per share. For those of you that have been following Motus for a long time, you also see that we've increased that payout ratio as well.
Our cash flows from operating activities is also at a stellar number, ZAR 1.9 billion, and that compares to only ZAR 186 million in the previous period. I always believe that cash is king. The accountants can cloud the numbers with provisions and everything else, but when you look at that cash number and ZAR 1.9 billion in just six months, yeah, it's really kudos to the Motus team who have gone over and above to be able to deliver such a stellar number that has been banked and able to strengthen the balance sheet for the six-month period.
